knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Component Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the continuous-LP epigraph construction for separable piecewise-linear objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a piecewise-linear component \(f_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is nonconvex, then \(\operatorname{epi}f_i\) is nonconvex and therefore cannot equal a polyhedron or a coordinate projection of a polyhedron. Thus its full epigraph has no exact formulation using finitely many continuous variables and linear constraints; an exact model generally requires additional disjunctive structure, such as integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex piecewise-linear component has a nonconvex epigraph, so its full epigraph cannot be represented by a finite continuous LP.
assumptions_latex: At least one component \(f_i\) is piecewise linear and nonconvex.
The formulation must reproduce the component's full epigraph using finitely many continuous linear constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_i\text{ nonconvex}\implies\operatorname{epi}f_i\text{ is not the projection of a finite-dimensional polyhedron}.

notation.meaning: Epigraph of the ith component function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composition of Bijective Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of objective-preserving bijective recovery under chained reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(T_{12}:X_1\to X_2\) and \(T_{23}:X_2\to X_3\) are bijections with inverses \(S_{21}\) and \(S_{32}\), and satisfy \(f_2(T_{12}(x))=f_1(x)\) and \(f_3(T_{23}(y))=f_2(y)\). Then \(T_{13}=T_{23}\circ T_{12}\) is an objective-preserving bijection with inverse \(S_{31}=S_{21}\circ S_{32}\). Hence bijective solution-recoverability, with specified objective-preserving maps, is an equivalence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-preserving bijective reformulations compose, so bijective recoverability is an equivalence relation.
assumptions_latex: \(T_{12}\) and \(T_{23}\) are objective-preserving bijections between the indicated feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{13}=T_{23}\circ T_{12}\text{ is an objective-preserving bijection with inverse }S_{21}\circ S_{32}.

notation.meaning: Forward recovery map from formulation i to formulation j.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Bijective Reformulations
Bijective Solution-Recovery Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reformulations whose feasible points and objective values correspond one-to-one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P=\inf\{f(x):x\in X\}\) and \(Q=\inf\{g(y):y\in Y\}\). The formulations are bijectively solution-recoverable if there exist maps \(T:X\to Y\) and \(S:Y\to X\) such that \(S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_X\), \(T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_Y\), and \(g(T(x))=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Consequently, \(T\) bijects the feasible sets, preserves objective values, and restricts to a bijection between the optimal-solution sets; \(S=T^{-1}\) recovers the original solution uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations have bijective recovery when inverse maps pair every feasible point uniquely and preserve its objective value, hence also pair their optima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) bijects \(X\) with \(Y\) and bijects \(\operatorname{argmin}_X f\) with \(\operatorname{argmin}_Y g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary-Dependent Objective Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates feasible-set projection equivalence from optimization equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\operatorname{proj}_xY\), and define the fiber value \(\phi(x)=\inf\{g(x,z):(x,z)\in Y\}\). Feasible-set projection alone does not make optimization over \(Y\) equivalent to minimizing an intended objective \(f\) over \(X\). Pointwise equality \(\phi(x)=f(x)\) gives equality of infima. Equality of recovered optimizer sets additionally requires that the fiber infimum be attained above every \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}_X f\); this attainment is automatic when \(Y\) is a polyhedron, \(g\) is linear, and the fiber optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection of feasible sets is insufficient for an auxiliary-dependent objective: fiber minima must reproduce the original objective, and optimal fibers must attain those minima for optimizer recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi(x)=\inf\{g(x,z):(x,z)\in Y\}\) is well-defined as an extended-real value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi=f\text{ on }X\implies\inf_Y g=\inf_X f;\quad \operatorname{proj}_x\operatorname*{argmin}_Yg=\operatorname*{argmin}_Xf\text{ if the relevant fiber infima are attained}.

notation.meaning: Infimum of the lifted objective over the auxiliary fiber above x.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Dependent Objective Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transitivity of Projection Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of nested polyhedral lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\), and \(Z\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p+q}\) satisfy \(X=\operatorname{proj}_xY\) and \(Y=\operatorname{proj}_{x,z}Z\). Then \(X=\operatorname{proj}_xZ\). If every formulation minimizes the same function of \(x\) alone, their optimal values agree and the projection onto \(x\) of the optimal set over \(Z\) equals the optimal set over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested projection-equivalent lifts compose, and an objective depending only on original variables preserves values and original-variable optimizers.
assumptions_latex: The compared objective depends only on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X=\operatorname{proj}_xZ,\qquad\operatorname{proj}_x\operatorname*{argmin}_{Z}c^{\mathsf T}x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{X}c^{\mathsf T}x.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the second auxiliary-variable block.

knowledge_statements.title: Transitivity of Projection Equivalence
Projection-Equivalent Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an extended formulation by exact projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of an LP and let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be a polyhedron in variables \((x,z)\). The lifted formulation is projection-equivalent to \(X\) when
\[X=\operatorname{proj}_x(Y)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^p,\ (x,z)\in Y\}.\]
If its objective is \(c^\top x\), independent of \(z\), then the original and lifted LPs have equal optimal values, and the projection of the lifted optimal-solution set equals the original optimal-solution set. Multiple lifted points may recover the same \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted formulation is projection-equivalent when eliminating its auxiliary variables gives exactly the original feasible set; auxiliary solutions need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two LPs have equal optimal values and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(\operatorname{argmin}_{(x,z)\in Y}c^\top x)=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}c^\top x\).

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection onto the original x-space.

children.title: Variable-Count Growth
children.top_down_role: Changes in variable count induced by an LP reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Count Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures the dimensional overhead introduced by an LP reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an original formulation has \(n\) scalar variables and its reformulation has \(n'\) scalar variables, define the additive variable growth by \(\Delta_v=n'-n\) and, for \(n>0\), the multiplicative growth by \(\rho_v=n'/n\). Introducing \(p\) auxiliary variables gives \(n'=n+p\), hence \(\Delta_v=p\) and \(\rho_v=1+p/n\). Replacing each of \(u\) unrestricted scalar variables by \(x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-\), with \(x_j^+,x_j^-\geq0\), increases the count by exactly \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-count growth is the difference or ratio between reformulated and original dimensions; p auxiliary variables add p, and splitting u free variables adds u.
assumptions_latex: The counts include all explicit scalar decision and auxiliary variables
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_v=n'-n\); adding \(p\) auxiliaries gives \(\Delta_v=p\), while splitting \(u\) unrestricted variables gives \(\Delta_v=u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable Count Is Not Equivalence-Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formulations may contain arbitrarily many superfluous auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a formulation with feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(Y_p=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^{n+p}:x\in X,\ z=0\}\). Projection maps \(Y_p\) onto \(X\), and \(x\mapsto(x,0)\) is a bijective objective-preserving recovery map for every objective depending only on \(x\). Nevertheless, \(Y_p\) has \(p\) more explicit variables. Since \(p\) is arbitrary, neither projection equivalence nor bijective recovery bounds variable-count growth without construction restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding fixed-zero auxiliary variables preserves even bijective recovery while increasing explicit dimension arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective is independent of \(z\).
All fixed-zero auxiliary variables are counted explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y_p\cong X\text{ by }x\leftrightarrow(x,0),\qquad\Delta_v=p\text{ for arbitrary }p\geq0.

notation.meaning: Equivalent lift with p fixed-zero auxiliary variables.

children.title: Constraint-Count Growth
children.top_down_role: Changes in row count induced by an LP reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Count Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures row-count overhead under standard LP form conversions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an LP description contain \(m_=\) equality rows and \(m_\leq\) inequality rows, with total \(m=m_=+m_\leq\). If a reformulation contains \(m'\) rows, its additive constraint growth is \(\Delta_c=m'-m\). Replacing every equality \(a_i^\top x=b_i\) by \(a_i^\top x\leq b_i\) and \(-a_i^\top x\leq-b_i\) yields an inequality-only description with \(m'=2m_=+m_\leq\), so \(\Delta_c=m_=\). Converting each inequality to an equality with one nonnegative slack variable preserves the row count: \(m'=m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting each equality into two inequalities adds one row per equality, while introducing one slack per inequality preserves the number of rows.
assumptions_latex: Constraint counts refer to explicit scalar rows
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality splitting gives \(\Delta_c=m_=\), whereas slack-variable conversion gives \(\Delta_c=0\).

notation.meaning: Numbers of equality and inequality rows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint Count Is Not Equivalence-Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent explicit descriptions can have arbitrarily different row counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Ax\leq b\) is an LP description, repeating any valid row \(k\) additional times leaves its feasible set unchanged while increasing the explicit constraint count by \(k\). More generally, redundant valid inequalities may be appended without changing the represented polyhedron. Thus mathematical or projection equivalence alone gives no finite upper bound on row-count growth; a bound must specify the construction and whether redundant rows are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate or redundant inequalities can increase an equivalent formulation's row count arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: Constraint count is the number of explicitly stored scalar rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{feas}(Ax\leq b)=\operatorname{feas}(A'x\leq b')\text{ while }m'-m=k\text{ for arbitrarily large }k.

children.top_down_role: Expansion of numerical coefficient ranges under representation changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient Magnitude Is Not Reformulation-Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical equivalence alone does not bound coefficient magnitude or encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any valid row \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) and scalar \(\lambda>0\), the row \(\lambda a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\lambda b\) defines the same halfspace. Equivalent LP descriptions can therefore have arbitrarily large or arbitrarily small nonzero coefficient magnitudes. With exact rational data, choices of \(\lambda\) having large numerators or denominators can also increase binary encoding length without changing the feasible set. Coefficient-growth bounds consequently require a specified reformulation and normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row scaling preserves feasibility but can change coefficient magnitudes and bit lengths arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: For the encoding statement, \(a,b,\lambda\) are rational and encoded exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\}=\{x:\lambda a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\lambda b\},\quad\text{while magnitude and encoding changes are unbounded over }\lambda.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Magnitude Is Not Reformulation-Invariant
Coefficient Magnitude Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracks numerical and encoding-size inflation caused by reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational LP data \(D\), define \(M(D)=\max\{|q|:q\text{ is a coefficient in }D\}\) and let \(L(D)\) be the maximum binary encoding length of a coefficient in lowest terms. For a reformulated data set \(D'\), coefficient growth is measured by \(M(D')/\max\{1,M(D)\}\) and \(L(D')-L(D)\). Equality splitting, sign reversal, slack insertion, and unrestricted-variable splitting introduce only copies, negatives, zeros, and coefficients in \(\{-1,1\}\); therefore \(M(D')\leq\max\{M(D),1\}\) and no copied coefficient acquires a larger encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Magnitude growth compares largest coefficients and bit lengths. Standard sign, slack, equality-splitting, and free-variable conversions introduce only copies and unit coefficients.
assumptions_latex: All input coefficients are rational and represented in lowest terms
Only the listed elementary reformulations are applied
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(D')\leq\max\{M(D),1\}\), with no encoding-length increase for coefficients copied from \(D\).

notation.meaning: Largest absolute coefficient in data set D.
Largest binary coefficient-encoding length in D.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity Pattern Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies nonzero-pattern changes under elementary LP reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Appending one slack variable to every inequality produces \([A\ I_m]\), whose nonzero count is \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m\). Splitting every variable as \(x=x^+-x^-\) produces \([A\ -A]\), whose nonzero count is \(2\operatorname{nnz}(A)\). Splitting every row \(Ax=b\) into opposite inequalities produces \([A^\top\ -A^\top]^\top\), again with \(2\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) nonzeros. These operations preserve the locations of original incidences but respectively add degree-one columns or duplicate column or row incidence patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slack variables add one nonzero per row; splitting all variables or all equality rows doubles the matrix nonzeros and duplicates incidence patterns.
assumptions_latex: No zero entries are stored explicitly
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Slack insertion gives \(\operatorname{nnz}([A\ I_m])=\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m\); complete variable or row splitting doubles \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\).

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero entries in A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme points and degenerate vertices of a polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent geometric characterizations for a canonical polyhedron in ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). If a defining inequality is active at \(\bar x=\lambda x'+(1-\lambda)x''\), where \(x',x''\in X\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), then it is active at both \(x'\) and \(x''\). A point \(\bar x\in X\) is an extreme point (vertex) if and only if it lies on \(n\) linearly independent defining hyperplanes, equivalently if it is not a strict convex combination of two distinct points of \(X\). A vertex through which \(q>n\) defining hyperplanes pass is degenerate, with order of degeneracy \(q-n\); a polyhedron having such a vertex is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active defining inequality at an interior convex combination is active at both endpoints. A feasible point is a vertex exactly when n linearly independent defining hyperplanes are active there, equivalently when it cannot be expressed as a strict convex combination of two distinct feasible points. A vertex lying on q greater than n defining hyperplanes is degenerate of order q minus n, and a polyhedron with such a vertex is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname{ext}(X)\iff \operatorname{rank}(G_{\mathrm{active}}(\bar x))=n\iff \nexists\,x'\ne x'',\ 0<\lambda<1:\ \bar x=\lambda x'+(1-\lambda)x'';\qquad \operatorname{degord}(\bar x)=q-n\ \text{when }q>n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and outcome regimes of a linear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers general LP feasible-set geometry and the alternatives highlighted by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear program \(\inf\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\), where \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is defined by finitely many linear equalities and inequalities, \(P\) is a convex polyhedron and the objective level sets are hyperplanes. If an optimum is attained, \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx\) is an exposed face of \(P\); it may be a single vertex, a positive-dimensional face, or all of \(P\). The problem has no minimizer when \(P=\varnothing\) or when \(\inf_{x\in P}c^Tx=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP has a convex polyhedral feasible set and planar objective contours. Its attained minimizers form an exposed face, ranging from one vertex to the whole feasible set. An empty feasible set gives infeasibility, while an objective unbounded below gives an unbounded problem with no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is polyhedral, and if }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^Tx\neq\varnothing,\text{ it is an exposed face of }P;\quad P=\varnothing\text{ or }\inf_{x\in P}c^Tx=-\infty\Rightarrow\text{no minimizer}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparsity bound for a polyhedral point-ray representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the finite extreme-point and extreme-direction representation of a nonempty polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has extreme points \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) and extreme directions \(d_1,\ldots,d_\ell\) as in the point-ray representation theorem. For every \(\bar x\in X\), there exist \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(\mu\ge0\) such that \(\bar x=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_jx_j+\sum_{j=1}^\ell\mu_jd_j\), \(\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j=1\), and at most \(\min\{n+1,k+\ell\}\) of the combined coefficients \(\lambda_j,\mu_j\) are positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the polyhedron has an extreme-point-plus-extreme-direction representation using at most the smaller of n + 1 and the total number of available generators as positive coefficients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedra, polytopes, and redundant inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite halfspace descriptions, the bounded-polyhedron terminology, and geometric redundancy of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron (polyhedral set) if it is the intersection of finitely many halfspaces; equivalently, \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Linear equations may be included because \(a^\top x=\beta\) is equivalent to \(a^\top x\le\beta\) and \(-a^\top x\le-\beta\). A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope. An inequality in a finite description is geometrically redundant if deleting it leaves the represented polyhedron unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is the intersection of finitely many halfspaces, equivalently a set described by finitely many linear inequalities. Linear equations can be represented by pairs of inequalities. A bounded polyhedron is a polytope, and an inequality is geometrically redundant when removing it does not change the represented set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:(a^i)^\top x\le b_i\}=\{x:Ax\le b\};\quad P\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow P\text{ is a polytope}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Point-and-Cone Representation of Polyhedral Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes polyhedral sets through a finite convex generator set and a finitely generated cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(P\) is polyhedral if and only if there exist a nonempty finite family \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) and a finitely generated cone \(C\) such that \[P=\left\{y+\sum_{j=1}^m\mu_jv_j\;\middle|\;y\in C,\ \sum_{j=1}^m\mu_j=1,\ \mu_j\ge 0\ (j=1,\ldots,m)\right\}=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}+C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is polyhedral exactly when it is the sum of the convex hull of a nonempty finite collection of points and a finitely generated cone.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a finitely generated cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is polyhedral}\iff P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}+C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-point and extreme-direction representation of a nonempty polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a nonempty polyhedron in nonnegative-variable inequality form; unboundedness determines whether extreme directions occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing\). Its extreme points form a nonempty finite set \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\). The set of extreme directions is empty if and only if \(X\) is bounded; if \(X\) is unbounded, it is nonempty and has finitely many representatives \(\{d_1,\ldots,d_\ell\}\). Moreover, \(\bar x\in X\) if and only if \(\bar x=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_jx_j+\sum_{j=1}^\ell\mu_jd_j\), where \(\lambda_j\ge0\), \(\mu_j\ge0\), and \(\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron defined by Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0 has finitely many extreme points and at least one. It has extreme directions exactly when it is unbounded, with finitely many extreme-direction representatives. Every point of the polyhedron, and only such a point, is a convex combination of its extreme points plus a nonnegative combination of its extreme directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X=\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}+\operatorname{cone}\{d_1,\ldots,d_\ell\},\qquad \{d_1,\ldots,d_\ell\}=\varnothing\iff X\text{ is bounded}.

children.title: Halfspace Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral representations through finite systems of linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Halfspace Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersection description of a polyhedron by closed affine halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed affine halfspace in \(\mathbb R^n\) is a set \(H(a,\beta)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^\top x\leq\beta\}\), where \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). A halfspace description of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a finite family \((a_i,\beta_i)_{i=1}^m\) satisfying
\[P=\bigcap_{i=1}^m H(a_i,\beta_i)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}.\]
The description may contain redundant inequalities and need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A halfspace description expresses a polyhedron as the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces, possibly with redundant inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:a_i^\top x\leq\beta_i\}=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\).

notation.meaning: Closed affine halfspace with normal a and threshold beta.
Matrix and right-hand side formed from the halfspace data.

children.title: Affine Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Affine subspaces or equality systems restricting the ambient geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes affine sets as solution sets of finite linear equation systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine description in \(\mathbb R^n\) is a system \(Ax=b\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), defining
\[L=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}.\]
If \(L\neq\varnothing\) and \(x_0\in L\), then \(L=x_0+\ker A\), so \(L\) is an affine subspace. Conversely, every affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\) admits such a finite equation description. If \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, its described set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent linear equation system describes an affine subspace equal to one solution plus the matrix kernel; inconsistent systems describe the empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x_0\in L\), then \(L=x_0+\ker A\); every affine subspace has a representation \(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\).

notation.meaning: Set described by the affine equations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Subspaces and Equality-System Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine subspaces as translates of linear subspaces and nonempty linear equality solution sets as translates of nullspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If S_0\leq\mathbb R^n and x^0\in\mathbb R^n, then S=S_0+x^0=\{x+x^0:x\in S_0\} is an affine subspace and \dim S=\dim S_0. In particular, x^0+\operatorname{span}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\} has dimension k when x^1,\ldots,x^k are linearly independent. If A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbb R^m, and \{x:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing, then for any x^0 satisfying Ax^0=b, \{x:Ax=b\}=x^0+\ker A. If the m rows of A are linearly independent, this affine solution set has dimension n-m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine subspace is a translate of a linear subspace and inherits its dimension. Every nonempty linear equality solution set is a translate of the coefficient matrix's nullspace; with m independent rows in n variables, its dimension is n−m.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_0+x^0\text{ is affine and }\dim(S_0+x^0)=\dim S_0;\quad \{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}=x^0+\ker A;\quad \operatorname{rank}(A)=m\Rightarrow\dim\{x:Ax=b\}=n-m

children.title: Mixed Equality–Inequality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Combined row descriptions separating affine restrictions from halfspace boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Equality–Inequality Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral descriptions containing both linear equations and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mixed equality–inequality description of a set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) consists of matrices \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(E\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) and vectors \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(d\in\mathbb R^r\) such that
\[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b,\ Ex=d\}.\]
It describes a polyhedron, possibly empty. The equation block restricts \(P\) to the affine set \(\{x:Ex=d\}\), while the inequality block intersects that affine set with finitely many closed halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed description defines a polyhedron using simultaneous linear inequalities and equations, intersecting an affine set with finitely many halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\cap\{x:Ex=d\}\) is a polyhedron, possibly empty.

children.title: Description Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence among alternative row descriptions of the same polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Description Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversions among halfspace, affine, and mixed descriptions of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For compatible finite-dimensional data,
\[\{x:Ax\leq b,\ Ex=d\}=\left\{x:\begin{bmatrix}A\\E\\-E\end{bmatrix}x\leq\begin{bmatrix}b\\d\\-d\end{bmatrix}\right\}.\]
Thus every mixed description has an equivalent inequality-only description in the same variable space. Conversely,
\[\{x:Ax\leq b\}=\{x:\exists s\in\mathbb R^m,\ Ax+s=b,\ s\geq0\},\]
so an inequality description is the projection of an affine equation system with nonnegative slack variables. Both conversions preserve the represented \(x\)-set; only the slack conversion enlarges the ambient variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equations equal pairs of opposite inequalities, while inequalities equal equations with nonnegative slacks; both conversions preserve exactly the original x-set.
assumptions_latex: All matrices and vectors have compatible finite dimensions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mixed descriptions convert exactly to inequality-only descriptions, and inequality descriptions are exact projections of slack-variable equality descriptions.

children.title: Unbounded Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean unboundedness, including its quantifier form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is unbounded if it is not bounded; explicitly, for every \(R<\infty\) there exists \(x\in P\) with \(\lVert x\rVert_2>R\). Under this definition an unbounded polyhedron is necessarily nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is unbounded when, for every finite radius, it contains a point outside the corresponding ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is unbounded}\iff \forall R<\infty\ \exists x\in P:\lVert x\rVert_2>R.\)

children.title: Recession-Based Boundary
children.top_down_role: Directional criterion separating bounded from unbounded polyhedral regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is bounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\};\qquad P\text{ is unbounded}\iff\exists d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:Ad\le0.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-cone characterization separating bounded and unbounded nonempty polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 2.7. Representation of bounded polyhedra, p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\). Define \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+td\in P\text{ for every }x\in P\text{ and every }t\ge0\}\). Then \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}\), and \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\). Equivalently, \(P\) is unbounded if and only if it has a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedron defined by Ax less than or equal to b, its recession cone is the set of directions d satisfying Ad less than or equal to zero. The polyhedron is bounded exactly when this cone contains only zero, and it is unbounded exactly when the cone contains a nonzero direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty polyhedron is the feasible set of an inequality system having no simultaneous solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonempty Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible inequality systems viewed as nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty when at least one vector satisfies every defining inequality, that is, when \(P\ne\varnothing\), equivalently \(\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(Ax\le b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is the feasible set of an inequality system with at least one simultaneous solution.

children.title: Feasibility-Regime Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural transition between inconsistent and consistent constraint descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Regime Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificate distinguishing feasibility from infeasibility of linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems has a solution: \(Ax\le b\) for some \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) for some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). In the second case, multiplying \(Ax\le b\) by \(y\) would force \(0\le b^{\mathsf T}y\), so \(y\) is a finite, directly checkable certificate that the polyhedron is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either the inequalities have a feasible point or a nonnegative Farkas multiplier certifies infeasibility, but never both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ax\le b\}=\varnothing\iff\exists y\ge0:\ A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Farkas alternative is the appropriate certificate for this leaf and the stated sign convention is mathematically consistent. However, no source is supplied, and the statement includes proof-style justification that must be removed once an authoritative theorem locator is available.

children.title: Affine Hulls
children.top_down_role: Smallest affine carriers associated with polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest affine subspace containing a nonempty polyhedron or set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing \(S\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{aff}(S)=\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R},\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\}\). For any fixed \(x_0\in S\), it also satisfies \(\operatorname{aff}(S)=x_0+\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set, equivalently the set of all finite affine combinations of its points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(S)=\bigcap\{L:L\text{ is affine and }S\subseteq L\}=x_0+\operatorname{span}(S-x_0).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-hull definition and equivalent representations fit the leaf, but no source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Affine Dimension
children.top_down_role: Dimension measured within the affine carrier of a polyhedral set.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension intrinsic to a nonempty polyhedron's affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine dimension is \(\dim(S)=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(S))\). If \(x_0\in S\), then \(\dim(S)=\dim(\operatorname{span}(S-x_0))\). Thus \(\dim(S)=k\) precisely when \(S\) contains \(k+1\) affinely independent points but contains no \(k+2\) affinely independent points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine dimension is the linear dimension of the translated affine hull and equals one less than the maximum number of affinely independent points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(S)=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(S))=\dim(\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)).\)

notation.meaning: Arbitrary base point in the set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-dimension definition and affine-independence characterization fit the leaf, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Ambient Dimension Gap
children.top_down_role: Difference between ambient-space dimension and affine dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Dimension Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension and the loss of ambient interior for lower-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(k=\dim(P)\). Its ambient dimension gap is the codimension \(n-k\). This gap is positive exactly when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\ne\mathbb{R}^n\), and exactly when the Euclidean interior of \(P\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron has positive ambient dimension gap exactly when it is lower-dimensional, equivalently when its ordinary Euclidean interior is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n-k>0\iff\operatorname{aff}(P)\ne\mathbb{R}^n\iff\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)=\varnothing.\)

notation.meaning: Interior in the ambient Euclidean space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a nonempty convex polyhedron, the codimension, proper affine-hull, and empty ambient-interior equivalences are correctly stated and the property kind fits the leaf. An authoritative locator supporting the dimension-interior equivalence is still required.

children.title: Ambient Interior
children.top_down_role: Interior geometry measured in the full ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary Euclidean interior of a polyhedron in its ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its ambient interior is \(\operatorname{int}(P)=\{x\in P:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B_2(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq P\}\), where \(B_2(x,\varepsilon)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert z-x\rVert_2<\varepsilon\}\). If \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is full-dimensional and its rows give nonredundant proper inequalities, then \(\operatorname{int}(P)=\{x:Ax<b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambient interior consists of points surrounded by a full-dimensional open ball lying entirely inside the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{int}(P)\iff\exists\varepsilon>0:\ B_2(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq P.\)

children.title: Polyhedral Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary strata of a polyhedron within its chosen ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient topological boundary of a closed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its ambient boundary is \(\partial P=\operatorname{cl}(P)\setminus\operatorname{int}(P)\). Every polyhedron is closed, so \(\partial P=P\setminus\operatorname{int}(P)\). Equivalently, \(x\in\partial P\) exactly when every open Euclidean ball centered at \(x\) meets both \(P\) and \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral boundary contains exactly the points whose every neighborhood meets both the polyhedron and its complement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial P=P\setminus\operatorname{int}(P).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ambient-boundary definition is correct for closed polyhedra and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Relative Interior
children.top_down_role: Interior geometry measured inside the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior taken within the affine hull of a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its relative interior is \(\operatorname{ri}(P)=\{x\in P:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B_2(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}(P)\subseteq P\}\). Thus the neighborhood is measured in the topology of \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\), not necessarily in all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Every nonempty polyhedron has nonempty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior uses neighborhoods inside the affine hull, so every nonempty polyhedron has relative-interior points even when its ambient interior is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(P)\iff\exists\varepsilon>0:\ B_2(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}(P)\subseteq P.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-interior definition and nonemptiness assertion are correct for nonempty polyhedra, and the definition kind fits the leaf. A specific authoritative source locator is required.

children.title: Ambient–Relative Interior Gap
children.top_down_role: Contrast between ambient and affine-hull interior regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient–Relative Interior Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes Euclidean interior from interior within a polyhedron’s affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. Its relative interior is the interior induced by the topology of \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\). If \(\dim P<n\), then \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\operatorname{ri}(P)\neq\varnothing\). If \(\dim P=n\), then \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(P)=\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)\). Thus ambient interior can fail to detect feasible interior points solely because the feasible set lies in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional nonempty polyhedron has empty Euclidean interior but nonempty relative interior; the two interiors coincide in the full-dimensional case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim P<n\Rightarrow \operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)=\varnothing\neq\operatorname{ri}(P)\).

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of P

children.title: Full-Dimensional Regime
children.top_down_role: Polyhedra whose affine dimension equals the ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Dimensional Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines full dimensionality in the LP decision space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is full-dimensional when \(\dim P=n\), equivalently when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\). For a nonempty convex set, this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)\neq\varnothing\). Hence a full-dimensional inequality-feasible region contains a point having a sufficiently small Euclidean neighborhood entirely within the region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is full-dimensional when its affine hull is the whole decision space, equivalently when it has nonempty Euclidean interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim P=n\iff\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\iff\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(P)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: dimension of the affine hull of P

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Regime
children.top_down_role: Polyhedra contained in a proper affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasible geometry confined to a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is lower-dimensional when \(d:=\dim P<n\), equivalently when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\) is a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). In this regime, \(P\) has empty ambient interior but nonempty relative interior. Its intrinsic geometry is therefore \(d\)-dimensional and should be expressed in coordinates on \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional polyhedron lies in a proper affine subspace and has intrinsic dimension smaller than the number of decision variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is lower-dimensional}\iff \dim P<n\iff\operatorname{aff}(P)\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^n\).

children.title: Affine-Hull Reduction
children.top_down_role: Passage from ambient coordinates to an intrinsic lower-dimensional representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a lower-dimensional LP in intrinsic affine coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\neq\varnothing\). Write \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=x_0+L\), where \(x_0\in P\) and \(L\) is a linear subspace of dimension \(d\). Choose \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) whose columns form a basis of \(L\), and define \(Q:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:A(x_0+Vz)\leq b\}\). Then \(z\mapsto x_0+Vz\) is an affine bijection from \(Q\) onto \(P\), \(\operatorname{aff}(Q)=\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\operatorname{ri}(P)=x_0+V\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(Q)\). For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) is equivalent, up to the constant \(c^{\mathsf T}x_0\), to minimizing \((V^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}z\) over \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinates on the affine hull transform the polyhedron into a full-dimensional polyhedron in its intrinsic variables and transform any linear objective by substitution.
assumptions_latex: \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) has columns forming a basis of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=x_0+VQ\), \(\operatorname{aff}(Q)=\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\operatorname{ri}(P)=x_0+V\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(Q)\).

notation.meaning: direction space of the affine hull
basis matrix for the affine-hull direction space

knowledge_statements.title: Active Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the constraints tight at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\), \(f\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ex=f,\ Ax\leq b\}\). For \(\bar x\in P\), writing \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) for row \(i\) of \(A\), the active inequality index set is \(I(\bar x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x=b_i\}\). The active constraint system at \(\bar x\) consists of \(Ex=f\) together with \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\) for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\). Its active normal matrix is formed by stacking the rows of \(E\) and the rows \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) indexed by \(I(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The active system at a feasible point contains all model equalities and exactly the inequalities that are tight at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(\bar x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x=b_i\}\).

notation.meaning: indices of inequalities active at the feasible point
row i of the inequality matrix A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active or Binding Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity of an indexed linear constraint at a specified point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an indexed linear constraint with coefficient vector \(a_i\) and right-hand side \(b_i\), where \(i\in M_1\cup M_2\cup M_3\), the constraint is called active, or binding, at \(x^*\) when \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x^*=b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear constraint is active or binding at a point when its left-hand side equals its right-hand side there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_i^{\mathsf T}x^*=b_i\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{constraint }i\text{ is active (binding) at }x^*

children.title: Redundant Constraint Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Row systems containing constraints removable without changing the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraint Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines redundancy of an inequality row in a polyhedral description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ex=f,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}\). Inequality \(i\) is redundant if deleting it leaves the represented set unchanged. With \(P_{-i}:=\{x:Ex=f,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_j\text{ for }j\neq i\}\), redundancy means \(P_{-i}=P\), equivalently every \(x\in P_{-i}\) satisfies \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\). A description is redundant when it contains at least one such row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is redundant when all other constraints already imply it, so deleting it does not change the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\text{ is redundant}\iff P_{-i}=P\iff P_{-i}\subseteq\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\}\).

notation.meaning: feasible set after deleting inequality i

children.title: Irredundant Constraint Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Row systems in which every listed constraint contributes to the represented set.

knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Constraint Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines descriptions in which every displayed constraint is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite constraint description \(P=\{x:g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for }i\in I,\ h_k(x)=0\text{ for }k\in K\}\) is irredundant if deleting any single displayed constraint strictly enlarges the represented set. Thus, for every \(i\in I\), the system without \(g_i(x)\leq0\) admits a point violating that inequality; and for every \(k\in K\), the system without \(h_k(x)=0\) admits a point violating that equality. Irredundancy is a property of the description, not solely of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A description is irredundant when deleting any one equality or inequality strictly enlarges its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{description irredundant}\iff\text{every displayed row is essential to its represented set}\).

children.title: Redundancy Removal
children.top_down_role: Structural passage from redundant descriptions to reduced descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Removal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removes implied inequalities using auxiliary linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a nonempty polyhedron \(P=\{x:Ex=f,\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i,\ i\in I\}\). Initialize \(J:=I\). For each \(i\in J\), solve \(v_i:=\sup\{a_i^{\mathsf T}x:Ex=f,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_j,\ j\in J\setminus\{i\}\}\). If \(v_i\leq b_i\), set \(J:=J\setminus\{i\}\); otherwise retain \(i\). Continue until every retained row has been tested against the current system. Output \(\{x:Ex=f,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_j,\ j\in J\}\), which represents \(P\) and is irredundant with respect to deletion of retained inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test each inequality by maximizing its left side without that row; delete it when the resulting optimum still satisfies its bound.
assumptions_latex: Each auxiliary linear program is solved with an exact infeasibility, boundedness, or unboundedness determination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:Ex=f,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_j,\ j\in J\}\) with no deletion-redundant retained inequality.

notation.meaning: current set of retained inequality indices
supremum in the redundancy test for row i

children.title: Description Minimality
children.top_down_role: Minimal row structure relative to a fixed class of constraint descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Description Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes minimality under deletion of displayed constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite constraint description \(D\) of a set \(P\), call \(D\) deletion-minimal if no proper subcollection obtained by deleting displayed constraints still represents \(P\). Then \(D\) is deletion-minimal if and only if it is irredundant. This notion does not assert minimum cardinality among all possible descriptions: algebraically different irredundant descriptions can exist, and introducing or eliminating equality structure may change the number of displayed rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deletion-minimality is equivalent to irredundancy, but it need not minimize the number of constraints across all possible formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite constraint description of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\text{ is deletion-minimal}\iff D\text{ is irredundant}\).

notation.meaning: the set represented by the description

children.title: Implicit Equalities
children.top_down_role: Equality restrictions encoded indirectly by inequality descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies inequalities that are tight throughout the feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\neq\varnothing\). Writing \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) for row \(i\) of \(A\), an inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\), with \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), is an implicit equality when \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\) for every \(x\in P\), equivalently when \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). Every implicit equality is an affine equation valid on \(P\); collectively, all affine equations valid on \(P\) determine \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\), and a maximal independent collection of their normal directions determines the loss of ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit equality is an inequality that is tight at every feasible point. It supplies an affine equation valid on the feasible set, although it need not be independent of other valid equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ is an implicit equality}\iff (\forall x\in P)\;a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\).

notation.meaning: affine hull determined by all affine equations valid on P

children.title: Constraint-Matrix Rank
children.top_down_role: Rank characteristics of equality and active-row systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Matrix Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates independent equality rows to feasible affine dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and suppose \(Ex=f\) is consistent. If \(r=\operatorname{rank}(E)\), then its solution set is an affine subspace \(x_0+\ker(E)\) of dimension \(n-r\). Thus only \(r\) linearly independent equality normals restrict affine dimension; dependent equality rows add no new direction restriction. When these equations describe \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\), the polyhedron has \(\dim P=n-r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent equality system of rank r defines an affine space of dimension n minus r; only independent equality rows reduce dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ex=f\}=x_0+\ker(E)\quad\text{and}\quad\dim\{x:Ex=f\}=n-\operatorname{rank}(E)\).

notation.meaning: rank of the equality constraint matrix
any solution of the consistent equality system

children.title: Rank Deficiency
children.top_down_role: Linear dependence within constraint descriptions or active systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines linear dependence among constraint rows and its geometric consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is row-rank deficient when \(\operatorname{rank}(E)<m\). For a consistent equality system \(Ex=f\), rank deficiency means that a nonzero \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies \(y^{\mathsf T}E=0\), necessarily with \(y^{\mathsf T}f=0\). Consequently, one may select \(r=\operatorname{rank}(E)\) independent rows whose equations imply all remaining rows; the full system and this subsystem have the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row-rank-deficient consistent equality system contains dependent equations; a rank-sized independent subset represents the same affine solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(E)<m\Rightarrow\exists y\neq0:\ y^{\mathsf T}E=0\text{ and }y^{\mathsf T}f=0\).

notation.meaning: a nonzero left-null vector witnessing row dependence

children.title: Hidden-Dimension Reduction
children.top_down_role: Affine-dimension loss associated with implicit restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The implicit equalities of \(P\) admit a full-row-rank representation \(Hx=h\) with \(\operatorname{rank}H=r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is affinely isomorphic to a polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^{n-r}\), and \(\dim P\le n-r\).

notation.meaning: A point satisfying the implicit equality system.
A matrix whose columns form a basis of the null space of H.
Coordinates in the reduced affine space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine elimination of equality-constrained directions in a finite-dimensional polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(x^0\) with \(Hx^0=h\), and let the columns of \(N\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-r)}\) form a basis of \(\ker H\). Every point satisfying the implicit equalities has the unique form \(x=x^0+Nz\), where \(z\in\mathbb R^{n-r}\). Consequently,
\[
P=\{x^0+Nz:z\in Q\},\qquad Q=\{z\in\mathbb R^{n-r}:ANz\le b-Ax^0\}.
\]
The map \(z\mapsto x^0+Nz\) is an affine bijection from \(Q\) to \(P\), so \(\dim P=\dim Q\le n-r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating r independent implicit equalities parametrizes the polyhedron uniquely in n-r coordinates and preserves its affine geometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Dimension Reduction

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\) is the largest linear subspace \(L\) satisfying \(P+L=P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality of a nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space of \(P\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:x+td\in P\text{ for every }x\in P\text{ and }t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P))\). If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), then
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad=0\}.
\]
This is the unique largest linear subspace \(L\) such that \(P+L=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions along which every point of the polyhedron can move by any signed amount while remaining feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Spaces

children.title: Pointed Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral sets without nontrivial lineality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional pointedness convention for nonempty polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polyhedron \(P\) is pointed if it contains no affine line. Explicitly, there do not exist \(x\in P\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
\{x+td:t\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq P.
\]
Equivalently, \(P\) is pointed if and only if its lineality space is trivial:
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is pointed when it contains no line, equivalently when its lineality space contains only the zero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

children.title: Nonpointed Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral sets possessing nontrivial lineality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is nonpointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary regime to pointedness for nonempty polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polyhedron \(P\) is nonpointed if it contains an affine line. Thus there exist \(x\in P\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
x+td\in P\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.
\]
Equivalently, \(P\) is nonpointed if and only if
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)\neq\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is nonpointed when it contains a line, equivalently when it has a nonzero lineality direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

children.title: Lineality-Based Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation of pointedness regimes through the presence of line directions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Trivial versus nontrivial lineality is the exact boundary between pointed and nonpointed polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pointedness boundary expressed through lineality.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\). The pointedness regimes are separated exactly by
\[
L=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P\text{ is pointed},
\]
and
\[
L\neq\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P\text{ is nonpointed}.
\]
For an inequality description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), this boundary is equivalently \(\ker A=\{0\}\) versus \(\ker A\neq\{0\}\), because \(L=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact boundary is whether the lineality space is trivial: zero lineality means pointed, while any nonzero lineality means nonpointed.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Based Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\).
\(N\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-\dim L)}\) has columns forming a basis of \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected polyhedron \(Q=N^{\mathsf T}P\) is pointed and satisfies \(P=NQ+L\).

notation.meaning: An orthonormal basis matrix for the orthogonal complement of L.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal quotient reduction removing all lineality directions.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose the columns of \(N\) orthonormally, so \(N^{\mathsf T}N=I\) and \(\operatorname{range}N=L^\perp\), and define
\[
Q=N^{\mathsf T}P=\{N^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}.
\]
Then \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-\dim L}\) is a pointed polyhedron. Moreover,
\[
P=NQ+L=\{Nz+\ell:z\in Q,\ \ell\in L\}.
\]
Thus projection onto \(L^\perp\), equivalently passage to the quotient \(\mathbb R^n/L\), removes precisely the lineality of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a polyhedron orthogonally away from its lineality produces a pointed polyhedron, while the original set is recovered by adding the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.title: Line-Free Reductions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacent Basic Solutions and Edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct basic solutions of the same linear-constraint system in \(\mathbb R^n\); feasibility is additionally required for the edge clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) be distinct basic solutions of the same system of linear constraints. They are adjacent if there exist \(n-1\) linearly independent constraints active at both \(x\) and \(y\). If the adjacent basic solutions \(x\) and \(y\) are also feasible, the line segment \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:0\le t\le1\}\) is called an edge of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct basic solutions in n-dimensional space are adjacent when they share n−1 linearly independent active constraints. If the adjacent solutions are feasible, the segment joining them is called an edge of the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: x,y\in\mathbb R^n\text{ are distinct basic solutions of the same linear-constraint system.}
\text{For the edge clause, }x\text{ and }y\text{ are adjacent and feasible.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\sim y\iff \exists\,n-1\text{ linearly independent constraints active at both }x\text{ and }y;\qquad x\sim y,\ x,y\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow [x,y]\text{ is called an edge of the feasible set.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral faces, dimensions, facets, and adjacent vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face taxonomy for a polyhedron in ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F\) of a polyhedron \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the set of points of \(X\) on which a nonempty collection of defining hyperplanes is active. If \(r(F)\) is the maximum number of linearly independent defining hyperplanes active at every point of \(F\), then \(\dim F=n-r(F)\). Thus vertices are zero-dimensional faces and edges are one-dimensional faces. Moreover, \(\dim X=n-r(X)\), and \(X\) is full-dimensional exactly when \(r(X)=0\). By the stated convention, \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) may be called improper faces and all other faces proper. If \(\dim X\ge1\), a facet is a proper face of dimension \(\dim X-1\). Two vertices are adjacent exactly when their joining segment is an edge; consequently they share \(n-1\) linearly independent active defining hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face consists of the feasible points satisfying a nonempty collection of defining inequalities at equality. If r(F) is the largest number of independent defining hyperplanes active throughout F, its dimension is n minus r(F). Vertices and edges are respectively zero- and one-dimensional faces. The polyhedron is full-dimensional exactly when no independent defining hyperplane is active throughout it. Under the given convention, the polyhedron and the empty set are improper faces; the others are proper. A facet has dimension one below that of the polyhedron. Two vertices are adjacent exactly when their connecting segment is an edge, and they therefore share n minus one independent active hyperplanes.
assumptions_latex: r(F)=\max\{\text{number of linearly independent defining hyperplanes active throughout }F\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim F=n-r(F),\quad \dim X=n-r(X),\quad X\text{ full-dimensional}\iff r(X)=0;\quad \dim(\text{facet})=\dim X-1;\quad u,v\text{ adjacent}\iff [u,v]\text{ is an edge}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Two standard face families are
\[
\mathcal F_{+}(P)=\{F\subseteq P:F\neq\varnothing\text{ and }F\text{ is supported}\}
\]
and the augmented family
\[
\mathcal F(P)=\mathcal F_{+}(P)\cup\{\varnothing\}.
\]
Both include \(P\), usually called the improper face. Some authors call every face other than \(P\) proper, thereby including \(\varnothing\); others reserve proper face for \(F\) satisfying \(\varnothing\neq F\subsetneq P\). Any theorem using proper or empty faces must state which convention applies.

knowledge_statements.title: Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-dimension definition valid for non-full-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The face \(F\) is a facet of \(P\) if it has codimension one relative to the affine hull of \(P\):
\[
\dim F=d-1,\qquad d=\dim P.
\]
Equivalently, \(F\) is a maximal proper face under inclusion: there is no face \(G\) satisfying \(F\subsetneq G\subsetneq P\). The dimension is relative, so full dimensionality of \(P\) in \(\mathbb R^n\) is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet is a maximal proper face, equivalently a face whose dimension is one less than the affine dimension of the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron of affine dimension \(d\ge1\).
\(F\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a facet exactly when \(\dim F=d-1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Dimension Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cover relations among nonempty polyhedral faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subsetneq G\) be nonempty faces of a polyhedron \(P\). Then \(\dim(F)<\dim(G)\). Moreover, \(G\) covers \(F\) in the face poset—meaning that no face \(H\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq H\subsetneq G\)—if and only if \(\dim(G)=\dim(F)+1\). Consequently, the dimension function grades the nonempty face poset.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Face Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inclusion lattice of all faces of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(P\), let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face, including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. Then \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) is a finite lattice. For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), their meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and their join is \[F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\},\] the smallest face containing both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a polyhedron form a finite inclusion lattice: meet is intersection, and join is the smallest face containing both faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\text{ is a finite lattice with meet }\cap\text{ and the displayed join}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Extremality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme points of a convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. A point \(x\in C\) is an extreme point of \(C\) if, whenever \(x=\lambda y+(1-\lambda)z\) with \(y,z\in C\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), it follows that \(y=z=x\). Thus \(x\) cannot lie strictly between two distinct points of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point cannot be expressed as a strict convex combination of two distinct points of the convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is extreme}\iff [x=\lambda y+(1-\lambda)z,\ 0<\lambda<1]\Rightarrow y=z=x.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Characterization Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent geometric and active-constraint tests for polyhedral vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(P=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:Au\le b\}\). For \(x\in P\), write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) and define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). The following are equivalent: \(x\) is an extreme point of \(P\); \(\{x\}\) is a zero-dimensional face of \(P\); \(\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\); \(x\) is the unique vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y=b_i\) for every \(i\in I(x)\); and the only \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(A_{I(x)}d=0\) is \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron, being an extreme point, having a singleton zero-dimensional face, having active normals that span the ambient space, being uniquely determined by the active equalities, and having a trivial active-constraint kernel are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is extreme}\iff \{x\}\text{ is a zero-dimensional face of }P\iff \operatorname{span}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}=\mathbb{R}^n\iff x\text{ is uniquely determined by the active equalities}\iff \ker A_{I(x)}=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: indices of constraints active at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Cost Identity, Optimality Test, and Unbounded-Ray Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a primal-feasible basis of a standard-form minimization linear program; includes the zero-step degeneracy boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\). Let \(\mathcal B\) be a basis with nonsingular \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\), let \(\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\), and suppose \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0\), \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). Define \(\lambda=B^{-T}c_{\mathcal B}\), \(s_{\mathcal B}=0\), and \(s_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^T\lambda\). If \(s_{\mathcal N}\geq0\), then \((x,\lambda,s)\) is optimal. If \(q\in\mathcal N\) has \(s_q<0\), set \(d=B^{-1}A_q\) and \(x_{\mathcal B}(t)=x_{\mathcal B}-dt\), \(x_q(t)=t\). For every feasible \(t\geq0\), \(c^Tx(t)=c^Tx+s_qt\), so the objective decreases strictly when \(t>0\). If \(d\leq0\), the ray is feasible for all \(t\geq0\) and the objective tends to \(-\infty\). Otherwise, \(\theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{\mathcal B})_i/d_i\) is the largest feasible step and makes at least one basic component zero; \(\theta\) may equal zero in a degenerate pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a primal-feasible basis of a standard-form minimization LP, solving the dual basis equations gives the nonbasic reduced costs. Nonnegative reduced costs certify optimality. If a nonbasic variable has negative reduced cost, increasing it along the associated basis direction changes the objective by its reduced cost times the step and therefore strictly improves the objective for every positive feasible step. If every component of the basis direction is nonpositive, this gives a feasible ray on which the objective tends to minus infinity. Otherwise, the minimum-ratio step is the largest feasible step and makes a basic variable zero; in a degenerate pivot that step can be zero.
assumptions_latex: B=A_{\mathcal B}\text{ is nonsingular},\quad \mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B
\lambda=B^{-T}c_{\mathcal B},\quad s_{\mathcal B}=0,\quad s_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^T\lambda
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_{\mathcal N}\geq0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\quad s_q<0\Rightarrow c^Tx(t)=c^Tx+s_qt;\quad d\leq0\Rightarrow \inf c^Tx=-\infty;\quad d\not\leq0\Rightarrow \theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}\frac{(x_{\mathcal B})_i}{d_i}.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-induced solutions of standard-form equality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a basis index set with complement \(N\). The basic solution associated with \(B\) is the unique vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) determined by \[x_N=0,\qquad x_B=A_B^{-1}b.\] It satisfies \(Ax=b\). For the standard-form feasible region \(P=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:Au=b,\ u\ge0\}\), this vector is a basic feasible solution exactly when \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis defines a basic solution by setting the nonbasic variables to zero and solving the basis equations; the solution is feasible for the standard-form region exactly when its basic entries are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a basis index set with complement \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_N=0,\ x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), and \(x\in P\iff A_B^{-1}b\ge0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic variables, columns, and basis matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology and representation associated with a standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x be a basic solution represented by a basic-index set I=\{B(1),\ldots,B(m)\}. Variables x_i with i\in I are basic and those with i\notin I are nonbasic. The columns A_i for i\in I are the basic columns and form the invertible basis matrix B=A_I. The basic-variable vector satisfies Bx_B=b and therefore x_B=B^{-1}b. Bases are identified by their sets of basic indices, so permuting the same indices does not produce a distinct basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a represented basic solution, the selected variables and columns are basic and the remaining variables are nonbasic. The selected columns form an invertible basis matrix, the basic values equal its inverse times the right-hand side, and reordering the same index set does not create a new basis.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a basic solution represented by }I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B:=A_I\text{ is invertible},\qquad x_B=B^{-1}b,\qquad I\text{ determines the basis independently of index order}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic characterization of an active constraint system that uniquely determines a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) and let \(I=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x^*=b_i\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Support Basis Lemma under Nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-size and feasible-basis consequences for a standard-form polyhedron with full row rank and only nondegenerate basic feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{x}\geq 0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and suppose every basic feasible solution of \(P\) is nondegenerate. For \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\in P\), let \(N=\{i:\bar{x}_i>0\}\). Then there exists \(B\subseteq N\) with \(|B|=m\) such that the columns of \(A_B\) are linearly independent and the corresponding basic solution is feasible. Consequently, \(|N|\geq m\). If \(|N|=m\), then \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) is a basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full row rank and nondegeneracy of every basic feasible solution, the positive support of any feasible point contains a feasible basis and has at least m indices. If it has exactly m indices, the point is itself basic feasible.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every basic feasible solution of }P\text{ is nondegenerate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists B\subseteq N:\ |B|=m,\ \operatorname{rank}(A_B)=m,\text{ and the }B\text{-basic solution is feasible}\right]\land |N|\geq m\land\left(|N|=m\implies\bar{\mathbf{x}}\text{ is a basic feasible solution}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Iteration of the Primal Revised Simplex Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form minimization iteration from a basic feasible solution; includes optimality and unboundedness termination tests and basis-inverse updating.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with a nonsingular basis matrix \(B=[A_{B(1)},\ldots,A_{B(m)}]\), an associated basic feasible solution \(x\), and \(B^{-1}\). Compute \(p^\top=c_{\mathcal B}^\top B^{-1}\) and \(\bar c_j=c_j-p^\top A_j\). If every \(\bar c_j\ge0\), terminate with \(x\) optimal. Otherwise choose \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\) and set \(u=B^{-1}A_j\). If \(u_i\le0\) for all \(i\), terminate with optimal value \(-\infty\). Otherwise set \(\theta^*=\min_{i:u_i>0}x_{B(i)}/u_i\), choose \(\ell\) attaining the minimum, and replace \(A_{B(\ell)}\) by \(A_j\). The new basic feasible solution satisfies \(y_j=\theta^*\) and \(y_{B(i)}=x_{B(i)}-\theta^*u_i\) for \(i\ne\ell\). To obtain the new inverse \(\bar B^{-1}\), apply row operations to \([B^{-1}\mid u]\) so that its last column becomes \(e_\ell\); its first \(m\) columns then equal \(\bar B^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a basis, its inverse, and the associated basic feasible solution, compute simplex multipliers and reduced costs. Nonnegative reduced costs certify optimality. Otherwise choose a negative-reduced-cost entering column and compute its transformed column. If that column has no positive component, the problem is unbounded below. Otherwise use the minimum-ratio test to select the leaving column, update the basic variables, exchange the basis columns, and recover the new basis inverse by row-reducing the augmented matrix formed from the old inverse and transformed entering column.
assumptions_latex: \min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\text{ is in primal standard form.}
x\text{ is the basic feasible solution associated with }B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c\ge0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\qquad \bar c_j<0\ \land\ B^{-1}A_j\le0\Rightarrow \inf c^\top x=-\infty;\qquad\text{otherwise the ratio-test pivot produces a new basic feasible solution and }\bar B^{-1}.
