knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible, Basic Feasible, and Degenerate Basic Feasible Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to the stated constraint system and the algebraic notion of a basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(x\) is feasible if it satisfies the given constraints. It is a basic feasible solution if it is both feasible and basic. A basic feasible solution is degenerate if it is also a degenerate basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector satisfying the constraints is feasible. A feasible vector that is also basic is a basic feasible solution, and it is a degenerate basic feasible solution when its underlying basic solution is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\in\mathcal F;\quad x\text{ is basic feasible}\iff x\in\mathcal F\text{ and }x\text{ is basic};\quad x\text{ is degenerate basic feasible}\iff x\text{ is basic feasible and degenerate}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finiteness of Standard-Form Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness of the vertex set without a boundedness assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\). Then \(K\) has at most finitely many extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible set of a full-row-rank standard-form linear system has only finitely many extreme points, even when it is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\operatorname{ext}(K)|<\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic and Basic Feasible Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-constraint definition for polyhedra described by linear equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be described by linear equality and inequality constraints, and let \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\). The vector \(x^*\) is a basic solution if every equality constraint is active at \(x^*\) and the active constraints include \(n\) constraints with linearly independent normal vectors. A basic solution is a basic feasible solution if it also satisfies every constraint defining \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic solution satisfies all equality constraints and has enough linearly independent active constraints to determine a point. It is basic feasible when it also satisfies every defining constraint.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is defined by linear equality and inequality constraints}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is basic}\iff\bigl(\text{all equalities are active at }x^*\text{ and }n\text{ active normals are linearly independent}\bigr),\qquad x^*\text{ is basic feasible}\iff\bigl(x^*\text{ is basic and }x^*\in P\bigr)

Thus vertices and basic feasible solutions are the same feasible points, although a degenerate vertex may correspond to several bases.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and finite bounds satisfy \(l_i<u_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bounded-variable basic solution fixes every nonbasic variable at one of its bounds and solves uniquely for the basic variables.

source_refs.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{l,u}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\). Choose \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), put \(N=B^c\), and partition \(N=N_l\mathbin{\dot\cup}N_u\). Set \(x_i=l_i\) for \(i\in N_l\), set \(x_i=u_i\) for \(i\in N_u\), and compute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N)\). This is a bounded-variable basic feasible solution exactly when \(l_B\le x_B\le u_B\). Every vertex of \(P_{l,u}\) admits such a representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-variable basis fixes each nonbasic variable at a lower or upper bound and solves for the basic variables; feasibility requires those solved values to remain within bounds.

children.title: Geometric Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Excess active facial structure at a polyhedral vertex.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and \(P\) contains a strictly positive point.
For \(F_i=\{x\in P:x_i=0\}\), the nonempty coordinate faces \(F_i\) are pairwise distinct facets and exhaust the facets of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vertex \(v\) is geometrically degenerate exactly when \(|\{i:v_i=0\}|>n-m\).

notation.meaning: Active coordinate-bound index set at a point
Coordinate face induced by the ith nonnegativity constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic vertex degeneracy in a standard-form representation whose coordinate faces correspond faithfully to the facets.

source_refs.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=\dim P=n-m\) and, for a vertex \(v\in P\), let \(Z(v)=\{i:v_i=0\}\). A vertex is geometrically nondegenerate when it is incident to exactly \(d\) facets of \(P\), and it is geometrically degenerate when it is incident to more than \(d\) facets. Under the stated facet-faithfulness assumption, the facets incident to \(v\) are exactly the distinct coordinate faces \(F_i\) with \(i\in Z(v)\). Consequently, \(v\) is geometrically nondegenerate exactly when \(|Z(v)|=n-m\), and it is geometrically degenerate exactly when \(|Z(v)|>n-m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is geometrically degenerate when it is incident to more facets than the dimension of the polyhedron. When the coordinate bounds represent the facets faithfully, this is equivalent to having more than n minus m zero components.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Degeneracy

children.title: Basis Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate basic-solution structure in an algebraic LP representation.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and \(B\) is a feasible basis for \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible basis \(B\) is degenerate exactly when \(x_i=0\) for some \(i\in B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible basis \(B\), let \(x_N=0\) and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\). The basis is nondegenerate if \(x_B>0\) componentwise. It is degenerate if at least one basic component is zero, equivalently if \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|<m\). Degeneracy is attached to the basis representation; however, if one basis representing \(x\) is degenerate, then every basis representing that same standard-form point is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible basis is degenerate when at least one basic variable is zero; equivalently, its basic feasible solution has fewer than the rank-many positive components.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis and Linear-Program Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The chapter-specific, primal basis-based meaning of degeneracy; other optimization contexts may use the term differently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B be a basis with basic index set \mathcal{B}, and let x be the basic feasible solution corresponding to B. The basis B is degenerate if and only if x_i=0 for some i\in\mathcal{B}. Under this convention, a linear program is degenerate if and only if it has at least one degenerate basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible basis is degenerate when at least one of its basic variables is zero. Under this basis-based convention, a linear program is degenerate when it has at least one degenerate basis.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a basis with basic index set }\mathcal{B}
x\text{ is the basic feasible solution corresponding to }B

children.title: Degeneracy Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between geometric and basis manifestations of degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and \(P\) contains a strictly positive point.
For \(F_i=\{x\in P:x_i=0\}\), the nonempty coordinate faces \(F_i\) are pairwise distinct facets and exhaust the facets of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a vertex \(v\), intrinsic geometric degeneracy, degeneracy of every basis representing \(v\), and \(|\operatorname{supp}(v)|<m\) are equivalent.

notation.meaning: Indices of positive components of the vertex
Coordinate face induced by the ith nonnegativity constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between intrinsic geometric degeneracy and basis degeneracy when the standard-form coordinate faces represent the facets faithfully.

source_refs.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) be a vertex of \(P\). Then \(\dim P=n-m\), \(|Z(v)|=n-|S(v)|\), and the stated facet-faithfulness assumption makes \(|Z(v)|\) the number of facets incident to \(v\). Hence the following are equivalent: \(v\) is geometrically degenerate; \(|Z(v)|>n-m\); \(|S(v)|<m\); and every feasible basis representing \(v\) contains a zero basic variable. When \(|S(v)|=m\), the vertex is geometrically nondegenerate and its unique representing basis is \(S(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the coordinate faces represent the facets faithfully, a vertex is geometrically degenerate exactly when every representing basis is degenerate, equivalently when fewer than m components are positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Correspondence

children.title: Correspondence Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation conditions under which the two degeneracy notions diverge.

assumptions_latex: Geometric degeneracy is interpreted intrinsically through facets of the feasible polyhedron, while basis degeneracy refers to a chosen equality-and-bound representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a dimensionally faithful, irredundant representation, geometric and basis degeneracy need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by forced-zero variables, redundant constraints, or representation changes.

source_refs.locator: 2.2. Extreme points, vertices, and basic feasible solutions p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(A=(1\;0)\), \(b=0\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:x_1=0,\ x\ge0\}\). At the vertex \(v=(0,0)\), the basis \(B=\{1\}\) is feasible and degenerate because \(x_1=0\). Intrinsically, however, \(P\) is a one-dimensional ray and \(v\) lies on exactly one proper facet, so it is nondegenerate relative to \(P\). The discrepancy occurs because \(x_1=0\) is forced throughout \(P\), strict feasibility fails, and \(\dim P\ne n-m\). Redundant equalities or bounds can cause the same failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis and geometric degeneracy can disagree when variables are forced to bounds or the representation is redundant, because active represented constraints need not be genuine facets.
knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Failure Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and \(v\) is a vertex of \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bases representing \(v\) are exactly the nonsingular \(m\)-subsets containing \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\); multiplicity greater than one is possible only if \(|\operatorname{supp}(v)|<m\).

notation.meaning: Family of bases representing the vertex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial description of all standard-form bases attached to one vertex.

source_refs.locator: Bases and Vertices p. 32

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{supp}(v)\). The family of bases representing \(v\) is \[\mathcal{B}(v)=\{B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|B|=m,\ S\subseteq B,\ \det(A_B)\ne0\}.\] Every \(B\in\mathcal{B}(v)\) yields \(v_{B^c}=0\) and \(v_B=A_B^{-1}b\). If \(|S|=m\), then \(\mathcal{B}(v)=\{S\}\). If \(|S|<m\), several nonsingular extensions of \(S\) may exist, producing multiple bases at the same degenerate vertex, although degeneracy alone does not guarantee that more than one extension exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex's bases are precisely the nonsingular rank-sized index sets containing its positive support. Nondegenerate vertices have one basis; degenerate vertices may have several.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Multiplicity at Vertices

children.title: Edge Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Incidence among edges through shared lower-dimensional faces.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron, and \(E_1,E_2\) are distinct one-dimensional faces of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The edges \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are adjacent exactly when \(E_1\cap E_2\) is a vertex of \(P\).

notation.meaning: Two distinct edges of the polyhedron
Set of vertices of the polyhedron

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial adjacency of distinct polyhedral edges.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Geometric Solution p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two distinct edges \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) of \(P\) are edge-adjacent when they are incident to a common vertex, equivalently when there exists \(v\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\) such that \(v\in E_1\cap E_2\). Since the intersection of two faces is a face, this is equivalent to \(E_1\cap E_2=\{v\}\) for some vertex \(v\). Sharing only a higher-dimensional containing face does not by itself make two disjoint edges adjacent under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct polyhedral edges are adjacent when they share a vertex; merely belonging to a common higher-dimensional face is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge Adjacency

children.title: Vertex Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Pairs of vertices connected through one-dimensional faces.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron, and \(u,v\) are distinct vertices of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent exactly when \([u,v]\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\).

notation.meaning: Closed line segment joining two vertices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex adjacency in the one-skeleton of a polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 2.2. Extreme points, vertices, and basic feasible solutions p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distinct vertices \(u,v\in P\) are adjacent if their segment \([u,v]=\{(1-t)u+tv:0\le t\le1\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\). Equivalently, there is a vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and scalar \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(c^Tx\le\alpha\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(\{x\in P:c^Tx=\alpha\}=[u,v]\). Thus adjacency is determined by the face structure, not merely by proximity or by a particular basis representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices are adjacent precisely when the segment joining them is an edge, equivalently an exposed one-dimensional face, of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Adjacency

children.title: Edge–Vertex Incidence
children.top_down_role: Endpoint and containment relations between edges and vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron, \(E\) is an edge of \(P\), and \(v\) is a vertex of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vertex \(v\) is incident to the edge \(E\) exactly when \(v\in E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence and endpoint structure of bounded and unbounded polyhedral edges.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Geometric Solution p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vertex \(v\) and an edge \(E\) of \(P\) are incident when \(v\in E\). If \(E\) is bounded, then there are unique distinct vertices \(u,v\) such that \(E=[u,v]\), and these are exactly the vertices incident to \(E\). If \(E\) is unbounded and contains a vertex, then there exist a unique incident vertex \(v\) and a nonzero extreme recession direction \(r\), unique up to positive scaling, such that \(E=\{v+tr:t\ge0\}\). Consequently, a bounded edge has two vertex incidences, while an unbounded edge has one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence means membership. A bounded edge has exactly two endpoint vertices, while an unbounded edge containing a vertex has one endpoint and one extreme recession direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge–Vertex Incidence

children.title: Degenerate Adjacency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Adjacency structure in the presence of geometric or basis degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) is a nonempty standard-form polyhedron.
\(x\in P\) is a degenerate basic feasible solution, so at least one basis representing \(x\) has a basic variable equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis adjacency and geometric vertex adjacency need not coincide: a simplex pivot may produce a different feasible basis representing the same vertex, and one geometric edge or adjacent-vertex pair may admit multiple basis-pivot representations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional standard-form LP; distinguishes combinatorial basis adjacency from geometric edge adjacency under degeneracy.

source_refs.locator: 2.2. Extreme points, vertices, and basic feasible solutions p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), and let \(x\) be a degenerate basic feasible solution. Degeneracy permits distinct feasible bases \(B_1\ne B_2\) to determine the same point \(x\). Consequently, a pivot between adjacent bases can have zero step length and leave the geometric vertex unchanged. Conversely, when two distinct vertices are joined by an edge, degeneracy can allow several choices of leaving or entering indices, hence several basis pivots, to represent that same geometric transition. Thus adjacency in the graph of feasible bases is generally neither an injective representation of vertex adjacency nor a one-to-one representation of edge incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate vertex, different adjacent bases may represent the same point, while a single geometric edge transition may have several pivot representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Adjacency Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\geq b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(y\in P\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to a defining inequality system for a polyhedral cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a nonzero \(x\in C\) is called an extreme ray when \(n-1\) linearly independent constraints are active at \(x\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremality within the recession directions of a convex set, identifying directions up to positive scaling.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedral cone if it is the intersection of finitely many halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes pass through the origin. Equivalently, for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le 0\}\); the \(i\)-th row of \(A\) is a normal vector to the hyperplane bounding the \(i\)-th halfspace.

Equivalently, it is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities; each matrix row is normal to the corresponding boundary hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of a Pointed Inequality Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes pointedness of a homogeneous inequality-defined polyhedral cone by extremality of the origin, absence of lines, and full rank of the defining normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(0\) is an extreme point of \(C\); (ii) \(C\) contains no line; (iii) among \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) there are \(n\) linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a homogeneous inequality-defined polyhedral cone, the origin is an extreme point exactly when the cone contains no line, equivalently when the defining normals span R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname{ext}(C)\iff C\text{ contains no line}\iff \operatorname{rank}[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]=n

children.title: Nonpointed Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones containing nontrivial linear subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpointedness for convex cones in finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonpointed precisely when it contains a nonzero linear subspace. Equivalently, there exists \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(d\in C\) and \(-d\in C\), or, equivalently, the line \(\{\lambda d:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}\) is contained in \(C\). Thus nonpointedness is exactly the condition \(C\cap(-C)\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is nonpointed exactly when it contains a line through the origin, equivalently when it contains some nonzero direction and its negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is nonpointed}\iff C\cap(-C)\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: set of negatives of elements of the cone

children.title: Cone Lineality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation of pointedness regimes through the cone lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Lineality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lineality-space criterion separating pointed and nonpointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its lineality space by \(L(C)=C\cap(-C)\). This set is the largest linear subspace contained in \(C\). The pointedness boundary is characterized by \(L(C)=\{0\}\): the cone is pointed exactly in this case, while \(\dim L(C)>0\) characterizes the nonpointed regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the largest subspace inside a cone. Its dimension is zero for pointed cones and positive for nonpointed cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is pointed}\iff L(C)=\{0\};\quad C\text{ is nonpointed}\iff\dim L(C)>0.\)

children.title: Pointed Quotient Structure
children.top_down_role: Lineality removal leading to a pointed quotient representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Quotient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed reduction obtained by quotienting a cone by its lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone, let \(L=C\cap(-C)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(\pi(C)\) is a pointed convex cone. Moreover, \(C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C))\), and if \(C\) is polyhedral, then \(\pi(C)\) is polyhedral in the quotient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by its lineality space produces a pointed convex cone, the original cone is exactly the inverse image of its quotient image, and polyhedrality is preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(C)\text{ is pointed},\quad C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C));\quad C\text{ polyhedral}\Rightarrow\pi(C)\text{ polyhedral}.\)

notation.meaning: canonical quotient map onto the space modulo lineality

knowledge_statements.title: Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator representation of cones in finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is finitely generated if there exist vectors \(v^1,\ldots,v^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i:\lambda_i\ge 0\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] The vectors are conic generators; the representation need not be irredundant or unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely generated cone consists of all nonnegative linear combinations of a finite list of vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}.\)

notation.meaning: set of all finite nonnegative combinations of vectors in the finite set V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finitely generated sets are polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse polyhedrality result for finite point-and-direction representations, including finite convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}+\operatorname{cone}\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
then \(Q\) is a polyhedron. In particular, for any finite family \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}\) is a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every set generated by finitely many point generators and direction generators is a polyhedron; in particular, the convex hull of finitely many vectors is a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is a polyhedron};\quad \operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}\text{ is a bounded polyhedron}

children.title: Cone Faces
children.top_down_role: Facial structure within polyhedral cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces of convex cones, including improper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone and let \(F\subseteq C\). Under the convention that the empty set is an improper face, \(F\) is a face of \(C\) if either \(F=\varnothing\), or \(F\) is a convex cone such that, for all \(x,y\in C\), \(x+y\in F\) implies \(x,y\in F\). For nonempty \(F\), this is equivalent to requiring that whenever a relative-interior point of a segment contained in \(C\) belongs to \(F\), both endpoints belong to \(F\). The sets \(C\) and \(\varnothing\) are the improper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convention, the empty set and the cone itself are improper faces. Every nonempty face is a convex subcone that contains both summands whenever it contains their sum; equivalently, it contains the endpoints of any cone segment whose relative interior meets the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\unlhd C\iff F=\varnothing\text{ or }[F\text{ is a convex cone and }\forall x,y\in C,\ x+y\in F\Rightarrow x,y\in F].\)

notation.meaning: F is a face of C

children.title: Extreme Rays
children.top_down_role: One-dimensional extremal generators of pointed cone structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme rays of pointed or nonpointed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone and let \(r\in C\setminus\{0\}\). The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\ge0\}\) is an extreme ray of \(C\) if \(R\) is a face of \(C\). Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\), the relation \(x+y\in R\) implies \(x,y\in R\). Consequently, a cone containing nonzero lineality has no extreme rays under this facial definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is extreme when any decomposition in the cone of a point on that ray uses only vectors on the same ray. Under this facial definition, a cone with nonzero lineality has no extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\mathbb{R}_+r\text{ is extreme}\iff[\forall x,y\in C,\ x+y\in R\Rightarrow x,y\in R].\)

source_refs.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

source_witnesses.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolution theorem for polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite vertex-and-ray representation of a nonempty polyhedron having an extreme point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\}\) be nonempty and have at least one extreme point. If \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\) are all extreme points of \(P\) and \(w^1,\ldots,w^r\) form a complete set of its extreme rays, then
\[
P=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x^i+\sum_{j=1}^r\theta_j w^j:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \theta_j\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a nonempty polyhedron having an extreme point is a convex combination of its extreme points plus a nonnegative combination of its extreme rays, and every such combination belongs to the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ has at least one extreme point}
\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}\text{ is a complete set of extreme rays of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}+\operatorname{cone}\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}

children.title: Extreme Line Generators
children.top_down_role: Generator structure associated with lineality in nonpointed cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Line Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line generators used to represent the lineality of a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedral cone with lineality space \(L=C\cap(-C)\). Choose a basis \(\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q\) of \(L\). Then every \(z\in L\) has the unique representation \(z=\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j\ell^j\) with \(\mu_j\in\mathbb{R}\), and \[L=\operatorname{cone}\{\ell^1,-\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q,-\ell^q\}.\] These basis vectors are line generators; unlike extreme rays, they are not canonically determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis of a cone's lineality space gives free-sign line generators, equivalently paired positive and negative conic generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap(-C)=\operatorname{span}\{\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q\}=\operatorname{cone}\{\pm\ell^1,\ldots,\pm\ell^q\}.\)

source_refs.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

source_witnesses.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

children.title: Face–Generator Incidence
children.top_down_role: Containment relations linking cone faces to extremal generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Face–Generator Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator membership characterizes nonempty faces of finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\). Then \[F=\operatorname{cone}\{v^i:v^i\in F\},\] where \(\operatorname{cone}\varnothing=\{0\}\). More precisely, if \(x\in F\) admits a representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), then every generator satisfying \(\lambda_i>0\) belongs to \(F\). Thus every nonempty face is generated by the original generators incident with it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face of a finitely generated cone is generated exactly by the listed generators lying in that face, with the conic hull of the empty family understood as the zero cone. Every positively used generator in a representation of a face point must belong to that face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v^i:v^i\in F\}.\)

notation.meaning: a member of the chosen finite generator family
the zero cone under the convention used in this record

children.title: Dual-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric roles of dual cones in polyhedral analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-inner-product convention for dual cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dual cone is \[C^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] The set \(C^*\) is always a closed convex cone. If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^{**}=C\). Furthermore, inclusion reverses under duality: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^*\subseteq C_1^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone contains vectors having nonnegative inner product with every primal cone vector; it is closed and convex, reverses inclusion, and satisfies bipolarity for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*\text{ is closed and convex};\quad C\text{ closed convex}\Rightarrow C^{**}=C.\)

notation.meaning: dual cone under the nonnegative pairing convention

children.title: Polar-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric roles of polar cones in polyhedral analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpositive-inner-product convention for polar cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its polar cone is \[C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] The set \(C^\circ\) is a closed convex cone. For nonempty sets \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), inclusion reverses under polarity: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ\). Moreover, \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C)\); hence if \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone contains vectors having nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original set. It is a closed convex cone, reverses inclusion, and its bipolar is the closure of the conic hull; consequently a closed convex cone equals its bipolar.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty when inclusion reversal is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C);\quad C\text{ closed convex cone}\Rightarrow C^{\circ\circ}=C.\)

notation.meaning: polar cone under the nonpositive pairing convention

source_refs.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

children.title: Dual–Polar Convention Mapping
children.top_down_role: Sign conventions, ambient spaces, plus translation between dual-cone terminology and polar-cone terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual–Polar Convention Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign conversion between dual- and polar-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt the conventions \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in C\}\) and \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). Then \[C^\circ=-C^*\qquad\text{and}\qquad C^*=-C^\circ.\] Hence any assertion expressed with one convention converts to the other by negating the dual variable; no geometric information is changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonnegative dual and nonpositive polar conventions, the polar cone is the negative of the dual cone, so formulas translate by negating the dual variable.
assumptions_latex: Dual and polar cones use the displayed sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=-C^*\) and \(C^*=-C^\circ\).

children.title: Halfspace Inequality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral descriptions expressed through halfspace inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Halfspace Inequality Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite closed-halfspace representation of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has a finite halfspace inequality description if there exist \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}.\] Such sets are precisely polyhedra. The description may contain redundant inequalities and is generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is exactly the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces, equivalently the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is a polyhedron}\iff P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ for some finite }m,A,b.\)

notation.meaning: i-th row of the inequality matrix

children.title: Affine Equality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Affine restrictions represented through equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Equality Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality-form description of an affine set, including the inconsistent case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the affine equality description is \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}.\] If the system is consistent and \(x^0\in P\), then \[P=x^0+\ker A=\{x^0+z:z\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ Az=0\}.\] If it is inconsistent, then \(P=\varnothing\). Thus every nonempty equality-described set is an affine translate of a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solutions of linear equalities form either the empty set or a translate of the null space of the coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\varnothing\) or \(P=x^0+\ker A\) for any \(x^0\in P\).

notation.meaning: Any feasible point of the equality system.

children.title: Mixed Constraint Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Representations combining halfspace inequalities with affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Constraint Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems combining weak linear inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^p\), a mixed constraint description has the form \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\},\] where \(Ax\le b\) is interpreted componentwise. Such a set is a polyhedron, possibly empty, because each equality can equivalently be replaced by the two inequalities \(Cx\le d\) and \(-Cx\le-d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed description intersects finitely many closed halfspaces with an affine equality set and therefore defines a possibly empty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\) is a polyhedron.

children.title: Point Generators
children.top_down_role: Point-based components of finite polyhedral generator descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Point Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point generators and their convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its point-generated set is the convex hull \[\operatorname{conv}(V)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] The members of \(V\) are point generators. A set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is generated by \(V\) alone precisely when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(V)\); such a set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point generators produce all convex combinations of a finite set; the resulting set is a bounded polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) consists exactly of the displayed convex combinations.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative convex-combination weights summing to one.

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

children.title: Recession-Ray Generators
children.top_down_role: Ray-based components capturing unbounded polyhedral directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Ray Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generators for the recession cone of a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\alpha r\in P\ \text{for every }x\in P,\ \alpha\ge0\}.\] A finite family \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\) is a recession-ray generator family when \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\mu_j\ge0\right\}.\] Nonzero members of \(R\) determine recession rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession-ray generators conically generate every direction along which a nonempty convex set remains feasible indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) generates the recession directions exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)\).

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

children.title: Mixed Point–Ray Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Generator descriptions containing both point components and recession-ray components.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Point–Ray Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex-plus-conic generator descriptions of polyhedra without explicit line generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite nonempty \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and finite \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the mixed point–ray description is \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\lambda_i,\mu_j\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Every displayed point belongs to a translate of the cone generated by \(R\), with its base in \(\operatorname{conv}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed generator description adds a conic combination of recession directions to a convex combination of base points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\).

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Representation of Polyhedral Sets p. 75

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Aware Generator Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator syntax separating bounded, one-sided recession, and two-sided lineality components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lineality-aware finite generator representation of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(D),\] equivalently \[x=\sum_i\lambda_i v^i+\sum_j\mu_jr^j+\sum_\ell\nu_\ell d^\ell,\qquad \lambda_i,\mu_j\ge0,\quad\sum_i\lambda_i=1,\quad\nu_\ell\in\mathbb{R}.\] The span term represents reversible directions and may be chosen equal to the lineality space \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap-\operatorname{rec}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This representation separates convex base points, one-sided recession rays, and freely signed generators of the polyhedron’s lineality space.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and nonempty; \(R\) and \(D\) are finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(D)\), with \(\operatorname{span}(D)=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) when lineality is represented exactly.

notation.meaning: Largest linear subspace contained in the recession cone of P.
Unrestricted coefficient of a lineality generator.

children.title: Minkowski–Weyl Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Organizer for bounded, pointed-unbounded, lineality-bearing, and conic representation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Polytope Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bounded case of the Minkowski–Weyl theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. Then \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron if and only if there exists a finite nonempty set \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V).\] Moreover, when \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron, \(V\) may be chosen as the finite set \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\) of all vertices of \(P\), giving \(P=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{vert}(P))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is a bounded polyhedron exactly when it is the convex hull of finitely many points; its vertices suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron if and only if \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) for some finite nonempty \(V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Unbounded Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski–Weyl representation specialized to nonempty pointed unbounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty pointed polyhedron. Then its vertex set \(V=\operatorname{vert}(P)\) is finite and nonempty, and there exists a finite set \(R\) containing one nonzero generator from each extreme ray of \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).\] If \(P\) is unbounded, then \(R\ne\varnothing\). Pointedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty pointed unbounded polyhedron is generated by its finitely many vertices and the finitely many extreme rays of its recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{vert}(P))+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for a finite nonempty extreme-ray generator set \(R\).

notation.meaning: Chosen generators of the extreme recession rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Aware Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski–Weyl representation retaining the maximal reversible recession subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap-\operatorname{rec}(P)\). There exist finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(V\ne\varnothing\), such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L.\] The rays may be chosen so that their images generate the pointed cone \(\operatorname{rec}(P)/L\). Conversely, every set having such a finite representation is a polyhedron whose lineality contains \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedron decomposes into finitely generated point, one-sided ray, and lineality components; the quotient recession cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\) for finite \(V\ne\varnothing\) and finite \(R\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone modulo its lineality subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Cone Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous Minkowski–Weyl theorem for convex cones in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the following are equivalent: \(K\) is polyhedral, meaning \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le0\}\) for some finite matrix \(A\); and \(K\) is finitely generated, meaning that some finite set \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\) satisfies \[K=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\mu_j\ge0\right\}.\] Lineality may be represented by including both \(d\) and \(-d\) among the generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is an intersection of finitely many homogeneous halfspaces exactly when it is generated by finitely many rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is polyhedral if and only if \(K=\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for some finite \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i s^i:k\in\{1,2,\ldots\},\ s^i\in S,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] It is the smallest convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(S\). Thus \(S\) convexly generates \(C\) precisely when \(C=\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Under the convention used here, \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull consists of all finite nonnegative combinations of one or more points whose coefficients sum to one and is the smallest convex set containing the generators; the convex hull of the empty set is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Hull Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic generation by unnormalized nonnegative finite combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its conic hull is \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\mu_i s^i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ s^i\in S,\ \mu_i\ge0\right\}.\] It is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\). Thus \(S\) conically generates \(K\) precisely when \(K=\operatorname{cone}(S)\). The zero vector belongs to every nonempty conic hull by taking all coefficients equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull contains all finite nonnegative combinations and is the smallest convex cone containing the generator set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Projection of Vectors and Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines projection onto the first k coordinates, including its existential characterization and preservation of nonemptiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(1\le k\le n\), define \(\pi_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k\) by \(\pi_k(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\). For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(\Pi_k(S)=\{\pi_k(x):x\in S\}=\{\bar x\in\mathbb R^k:\exists z\in\mathbb R^{n-k}\text{ such that }(\bar x,z)\in S\}\). Moreover, \(S\neq\varnothing\) if and only if \(\Pi_k(S)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate projection retains the first k coordinates. A retained vector is in the projected set exactly when it extends to a vector in the original set, and the projection is nonempty exactly when the original set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_k(S)=\{\pi_k(x):x\in S\}=\{\bar x\in\mathbb R^k:\exists z\in\mathbb R^{n-k},\ (\bar x,z)\in S\},\qquad S\neq\varnothing\iff\Pi_k(S)\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear and let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Its linear image is \[L(P):=\{Lx:x\in P\}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\exists x\in P,\ y=Lx\}.\] Equivalently, define the graph lift \(G_L(P):=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+m}:x\in P,\ y=Lx\}\). Then \(L(P)=\pi_y(G_L(P))\). Thus every general linear image can be expressed as a coordinate projection after adjoining image variables and linear graph equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image equals the coordinate projection of the set obtained by adjoining variables constrained to equal the linear map.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the rows into \(I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}\), \(I_-=\{i:\alpha_i<0\}\), and \(I_0=\{i:\alpha_i=0\}\). Each row in \(I_+\) gives \(t\leq u_i(x):=(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)/\alpha_i\), and each row in \(I_-\) gives \(t\geq\ell_j(x):=(b_j-a_j^{\mathsf T}x)/\alpha_j\). Retain \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\) for \(i\in I_0\), and add \(\ell_j(x)\leq u_i(x)\) for every \((i,j)\in I_+\times I_-\). The resulting system describes exactly the projection onto \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To eliminate one variable, retain zero-coefficient rows and compare every induced lower bound with every induced upper bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fourier–Motzkin Elimination of One Variable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs inequalities in the retained variables by comparing every lower bound with every upper bound on the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Tx\ge b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(\bar x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})\). Rewrite each constraint as \(x_n\ge d_i+f_i^T\bar x\) when \(a_{in}>0\), as \(x_n\le d_j+f_j^T\bar x\) when \(a_{jn}<0\), or as \(0\ge d_k+f_k^T\bar x\) when \(a_{kn}=0\). Construct \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}\) using \(d_j+f_j^T\bar x\ge d_i+f_i^T\bar x\) for every pair with \(a_{in}>0>a_{jn}\), together with all constraints corresponding to \(a_{kn}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify the inequalities as lower bounds, upper bounds, or constraints independent of the variable being eliminated. Compare every lower bound with every upper bound and retain every independent constraint to obtain an inequality system in the remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\left\{\bar x\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:d_j+f_j^T\bar x\ge d_i+f_i^T\bar x\ \forall(i,j)\text{ with }a_{in}>0>a_{jn},\ 0\ge d_k+f_k^T\bar x\ \forall k\text{ with }a_{kn}=0\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a nonempty system \(Q=\{x:Cx\leq d\}\), row \(c_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq d_k\) is redundant precisely when it is implied by the remaining rows: \[\sup\{c_k^{\mathsf T}x:C_{-k}x\leq d_{-k}\}\leq d_k.\] If the remaining subsystem is nonempty, linear programming duality gives the equivalent multiplier condition: there exists \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \(\lambda^{\mathsf T}C_{-k}=c_k^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\lambda^{\mathsf T}d_{-k}\leq d_k\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected inequality is redundant exactly when the remaining inequalities imply it; an LP bound or nonnegative multiplier certifies this implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Elimination-Induced Description Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw inequality-count upper bounds before duplicate and redundancy removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At elimination step \(r\), let \(m_r=p_r+q_r+z_r\), where \(p_r\), \(q_r\), and \(z_r\) count inequalities having positive, negative, and zero coefficients, respectively, for the variable being eliminated. Before duplicate or redundancy removal, the next description has at most \[m_{r+1}\leq p_rq_r+z_r\leq \left\lfloor\frac{(m_r-z_r)^2}{4}\right\rfloor+z_r\] inequalities. Consequently, if \(z_r=0\) at every one of the first \(k\) elimination steps, then \(m_{r+1}\leq m_r^2/4\) and hence \[m_k\leq4\left(\frac{m_0}{4}\right)^{2^k}.\] This is a doubly exponential upper envelope in the number of eliminated variables; it does not by itself assert that the bound is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One elimination produces at most one inequality for each positive-negative row pair, plus the zero-coefficient rows. If no zero-coefficient rows occur in the successive steps, the resulting recurrence gives a doubly exponential upper envelope, without asserting that every instance attains it.
assumptions_latex: \(k\geq 1\) elimination steps are performed, starting from \(m_0\) inequalities.
At step \(r\), the current \(m_r=p_r+q_r+z_r\) inequalities split into \(p_r\), \(q_r\), and \(z_r\) rows with positive, negative, and zero eliminated-variable coefficients.
For the iterated closed-form bound, \(z_r=0\) for \(r=0,\ldots,k-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_{r+1}\leq p_rq_r+z_r\leq\left\lfloor(m_r-z_r)^2/4\right\rfloor+z_r\); if \(z_r=0\) for \(r=0,\ldots,k-1\), then \(m_k\leq4(m_0/4)^{2^k}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite inequality description \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Cx\leq d\}\) is irredundant when deleting any one row strictly enlarges the represented set. The lift represents the original-space set obtained by retaining only \(x\), namely \(\pi_x(Q)\). Distinct lifted descriptions may have different auxiliary dimensions and inequality counts while projecting to the same set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lifted polyhedron \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) and an original-space polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) form a lift–projection representation pair exactly when \[P=\pi_x(Q),\] or, equivalently, when \[x\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q.\] Writing \(Q=\{(x,y):Ex+Fy\leq g\}\) therefore yields the existential description \(P=\{x:\exists y,\ Ex+Fy\leq g\}\); eliminating \(y\) yields an inequality description solely in \(x\) without changing the represented set.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Lifted Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-size extended formulations for families of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_n}\) be a family of polyhedra. A compact lifted description of \(P_n\) is a system \[Q_n=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_n+r_n}:A_nx+B_ny\le b_n\}\] such that \(P_n=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q_n\}\) and both the number of inequalities defining \(Q_n\) and the auxiliary dimension \(r_n\) are bounded by a polynomial in the chosen encoding parameter \(n\). Thus projection may describe \(P_n\) with substantially fewer inequalities than any formulation using only the original variables.

assumptions_latex: Description size counts inequalities and auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_n)\) with polynomially bounded lifted size.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outcome classification for a minimization-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the linear program \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\), where \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\). It is in the infeasible regime exactly when \(P=\varnothing\). In that regime no feasible solution, optimal solution, or finite optimal value exists. Under the extended-real minimization convention, its value is \(+\infty\); this convention distinguishes infeasibility from objective unboundedness, whose value is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization LP is infeasible exactly when its constraint system has no solution; conventionally its value is positive infinity.
assumptions_latex: The LP is interpreted as a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infeasible regime is equivalent to \(P=\varnothing\), with value \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Optimal-Value Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-value outcome for a nonempty polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), the linear program \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is in the finite optimal-value regime exactly when \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for every recession direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\). Under these conditions the infimum is a real number and is attained: there exist \(v^\star\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(x^\star\in P\) such that \(v^\star=c^{\mathsf T}x^\star=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible polyhedral LP has a finite attained minimum exactly when the objective does not decrease along any recession direction.
assumptions_latex: The objective is linear and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is finite and attained if and only if \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for all \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Unboundedness Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward objective unboundedness for a feasible minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. The minimization problem \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is objective-unbounded exactly when there exists \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Indeed, for every \(x^0\in P\), the ray \(x^0+td\) remains feasible for all \(t\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}(x^0+td)\to-\infty\). Hence the extended-real optimal value is \(-\infty\) and no optimal solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimization LP is unbounded below exactly when some feasible recession direction strictly decreases the objective.
assumptions_latex: The problem is in minimization form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value is \(-\infty\) if and only if some \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Feasible Set with Finite Optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates feasible-set unboundedness from objective unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), the minimization problem \(\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) has an unbounded feasible set but a finite optimum exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\ne\{0\}\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\). knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the minimizers of a finite-valued LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron and suppose \(v^\star=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is finite. The optimal set \[F^\star=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^\star\}\] is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\). Equivalently, if \(z=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in F^\star\) for \(x,y\in P\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), then \(x,y\in F^\star\). Every point of this face is optimal, and no point of \(P\setminus F^\star\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an LP has a finite optimum, all minimizers form the nonempty exposed face where the objective-supporting hyperplane meets the feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^\star=P\cap\{x:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^\star\}\) is a nonempty exposed face of \(P\).

children.title: Unique Optimal Solutions
children.top_down_role: Geometric regime in which the optimal solution set contains a single point.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Optimal Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-dimensional optimal-face regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the linear program over the polyhedron \(P\) has finite optimal value \(v^\star\) and optimal face \(F^\star=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^\star\}\). The optimal solution is unique exactly when \(F^\star\) is a singleton. Equivalently, there exists \(x^\star\in P\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}x>c^{\mathsf T}x^\star\) for every \(x\in P\setminus\{x^\star\}\). In this regime \(F^\star=\{x^\star\}\) and \(\dim F^\star=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP has a unique optimizer exactly when its optimal face consists of one point, equivalently when every other feasible point has strictly worse objective value.
assumptions_latex: The LP has a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniqueness is equivalent to \(F^\star=\{x^\star\}\), hence to \(\dim F^\star=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Alternate Optimal Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-dimensional optimal-face regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an LP has finite optimal value and optimal face \(F^\star\). Alternate optimal solutions exist exactly when \(F^\star\) contains two distinct points \(x^1\ne x^2\). In that case every convex combination \(\lambda x^1+(1-\lambda)x^2\), with \(0\le\lambda\le1\), is feasible and optimal, so there are infinitely many optimal solutions and \(\dim F^\star\ge1\). Conversely, if \(\dim F^\star\ge1\), then \(F^\star\) contains distinct points and the optimum is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct optimizers generate an entire optimal line segment; alternate optima therefore occur exactly when the optimal face has positive dimension.
assumptions_latex: The LP has a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alternate optima exist if and only if \(\dim F^\star\ge1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity classification by affine dimension of the optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F^\star\) be the nonempty optimal face of an LP with finite optimum, and let \(k=\dim F^\star\), where dimension means affine dimension. Then \(0\le k\le\dim P\). The regime \(k=0\) is precisely unique optimality; every regime \(k\ge1\) has infinitely many optimal solutions. If \(k=\dim P\), then \(F^\star=P\), so the objective is constant on \(P\). Intermediate values \(0<k<\dim P\) correspond to proper positive-dimensional optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine dimension of the optimal face classifies uniqueness, alternate optima, and the case where every feasible point is optimal.
assumptions_latex: The LP has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\dim F^\star\le\dim P\), with the stated uniqueness, intermediate-face, and full-face regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness criterion for a nonempty optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F^\star\) be the nonempty optimal face of a finite-valued LP over a polyhedron \(P\). The face \(F^\star\) is bounded exactly when its recession cone is trivial: \(\operatorname{rec}(F^\star)=\{0\}\). Since \(F^\star\) is a polyhedron, boundedness makes it a polytope. It may nevertheless have positive dimension and multiple optimal vertices; boundedness of the optimal face does not imply uniqueness of the optimal solution.

assumptions_latex: \(F^\star\) is a nonempty polyhedral optimal face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^\star\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(F^\star)=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness criterion for a finite-valued LP's optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F^\star\) be the nonempty optimal face of an LP over a polyhedron \(P\). The face is unbounded exactly when there exists a nonzero direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\). For every \(x^\star\in F^\star\), the ray \(x^\star+td\), \(t\ge0\), then lies in \(F^\star\). Thus infinitely many optimal solutions escape to infinity while the optimal objective value remains finite and constant along the ray.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^\star\) is unbounded if and only if some nonzero \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) has \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Structure of Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recession-cone formula for an LP optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron, and suppose \(F^\star=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^\star\}\) is its nonempty optimal face for minimization. Then \[\operatorname{rec}(F^\star)=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(P):c^{\mathsf T}d=0\}=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap c^\perp.\] Finite optimality guarantees \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) on \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\); precisely the zero-slope directions remain recession directions of the optimal face. Consequently, \(F^\star\) is bounded exactly when this intersection equals \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of the optimal face consists exactly of feasible recession directions along which the objective has zero slope.
assumptions_latex: The minimization LP has a finite attained optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(F^\star)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap c^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I_{F^*}:=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\text{ for every }x\in F^*\}\). The relative interior of the optimal face consists exactly of those optimal points at which every inequality not identically active on that face is strict:
\[
\operatorname{ri}(F^*)=\{x\in F^*:a_i^{\mathsf T}x<b_i\text{ for all }i\notin I_{F^*}\}.
\]
Thus all points in \(\operatorname{ri}(F^*)\) have precisely the inequalities indexed by \(I_{F^*}\) active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative-interior optimal solutions are exactly those having strict slack in every inequality that is not active throughout the entire optimal face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. If \(P\) contains no affine line, or equivalently if its lineality space satisfies \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\), then \(P\) has a vertex. Equivalently, there exists \(v\in P\) such that whenever \(v=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\) with \(x,y\in P\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), one has \(x=y=v\). Boundedness is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex, even when it is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointed-Polyhedron Vertex Existence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Criteria for Extreme-Point Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a nonempty polyhedron represented by finitely many inequalities, characterizes extreme-point existence by absence of affine lines and full rank of the constraint normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be nonempty. Then the following are equivalent: \(P\) has an extreme point; \(P\) contains no line; and the family \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) contains \(n\) linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron has an extreme point exactly when it contains no affine line, equivalently when its constraint-normal family contains n linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ has an extreme point}\iff P\text{ contains no line}\iff \exists i_1,\ldots,i_n\text{ such that }a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_n}\text{ are linearly independent}

P=\operatorname{conv}(V(P)).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P):=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+td\in P\text{ for every }x\in P\text{ and every }t\in\mathbb{R}\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P))\). If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), then \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{d:Ad=0\}=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space contains directions along which every feasible point can move arbitrarily far in both signs while remaining feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Theorem of Linear Programming in Standard Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of basic feasible representatives for feasible and optimal standard-form linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x:\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf x\geq\mathbf0\}\), where \(\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf A)=m\). If the program has a feasible solution, then it has a basic feasible solution. If it has an optimal feasible solution, then it has an optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard-form linear program whose constraint matrix has full row rank, feasibility implies the existence of a basic feasible solution, and existence of an optimal feasible solution implies the existence of an optimal basic feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: \min\{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x:\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf x\geq\mathbf0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists\mathbf x\geq\mathbf0:\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\bigr)\Rightarrow\bigl(\exists\text{ a basic feasible solution}\bigr),\qquad \bigl(\exists\text{ an optimal feasible solution}\bigr)\Rightarrow\bigl(\exists\text{ an optimal basic feasible solution}\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\), where \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty pointed polyhedron. If its value \(v^*\) is finite, then the minimum is attained and the optimal face contains a vertex of \(P\). Hence there exists a vertex \(x^*\in P\) such that
\[
c^{\mathsf T}x^*=v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective with finite value over a nonempty pointed polyhedron attains that value at a vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), a point \(x\in P\) is a vertex if and only if it is a basic feasible solution: there is \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\), nonsingular \(A_B\), and complement \(N\), such that \(x_N=0\) and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\). If the LP has finite optimal value, at least one such basic feasible solution is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In full-row-rank standard form, vertices are exactly basic feasible solutions, and a finite optimum is attained by one of them.

notation.meaning: Finite infimum of the linear objective.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If
\[
v^*:=\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x
\]
is finite, then the infimum is attained: there exists \(x^*\in P\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=v^*\). Thus a linear program over a nonempty polyhedron cannot have a finite but unattained optimal value, although its optimal set may be unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective over a nonempty polyhedron always attains its infimum whenever that infimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Optimum Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the minimization problem \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is unbounded below if and only if there exists \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). In that case, for every \(x\in P\) and \(t\ge0\), one has \(x+td\in P\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}(x+td)\to-\infty\). If no such direction exists, the value is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP is unbounded below exactly when its recession cone contains a direction that strictly decreases the objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Improving Recession-Direction Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Nontrivial lineality prevents vertex optimality even when the optimum is finite and attained. Indeed, let
\[
P_0:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^2:v\ge0\},\qquad c:=(0,1).
\]
Then \(\operatorname{lin}(P_0)=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\), the minimum of \(c^{\mathsf T}(u,v)=v\) equals \(0\), and the optimal set is \(\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\); nevertheless \(P_0\) has no vertices. More generally, boundedness below requires \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{lin}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality can coexist with a finite attained optimum, but then no feasible or optimal point is a vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: No-Vertex Lineality Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\varnothing\) if and only if there exists \(y\ge0\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-type separation certificate for an inequality-form LP system.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible:
\[
Ax\le b,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
y\ge0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Consequently \(P=\varnothing\) if and only if such a multiplier \(y\) exists. The vector \(y\) is a directly checkable infeasibility certificate and represents a strict separating functional between the attainable inequality image and the required right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality system is infeasible exactly when a nonnegative multiplier combines its left sides to zero and its right sides to a negative number.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Based Infeasibility Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Improving-Ray Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness certificate for a standard-form minimization LP with a known feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the linear program \\(\\inf\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge 0\\}\\). An improving-ray certificate is a pair \\((\\bar x,d)\\) satisfying \\(A\\bar x=b\\), \\(\\bar x\\ge0\\), \\(Ad=0\\), \\(d\\ge0\\), and \\(c^\\top d<0\\). For every \\(t\\ge0\\), the point \\(\\bar x+td\\) is feasible and \\(c^\\top(\\bar x+td)=c^\\top\\bar x+t c^\\top d\\). Consequently, the objective tends to \\(-\\infty\\) as \\(t\\to\\infty\\), so the LP is unbounded below. All certificate conditions are checkable by matrix-vector operations and componentwise comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and a feasible recession direction with strictly negative objective slope certify that the minimization LP is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The LP is interpreted as a minimization problem over \\(\\{x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\).

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Optimality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane certificate for minimizing a linear functional over an inequality-form polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(P=\\{x\\in\\mathbb R^n:Ax\\ge b\\}\\) and consider minimizing \\(c^\\top x\\) over \\(P\\). A supporting-hyperplane optimality certificate for \\(x^*\\) is a vector \\(\\lambda\\ge0\\) such that \\(Ax^*\\ge b\\), \\(A^\\top\\lambda=c\\), and \\(\\lambda^\\top(Ax^*-b)=0\\). These finite equalities and inequalities imply \\(c^\\top x\\ge c^\\top x^*\\) for every \\(x\\in P\\). Hence \\(P\\) lies in the closed halfspace \\(\\{x:c^\\top x\\ge c^\\top x^*\\}\\), whose boundary hyperplane supports \\(P\\) at \\(x^*\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and nonnegative multipliers representing the objective normal and satisfying complementary slackness certify a supporting hyperplane and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(x^*\\in\\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\\in P}c^\\top x\\), and \\(\\{x:c^\\top x=c^\\top x^*\\}\\) supports \\(P\\) at \\(x^*\\).

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Optimality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost optimality certificate for a feasible basis of a standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \\(\\min\\{c^\\top x:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}\\), where \\(A\\) has full row rank. Let the columns be partitioned as \\(A=[B\\;N]\\), with \\(B\\) nonsingular, and partition \\(c=(c_B,c_N)\\). Define \\(x_B=B^{-1}b\\), \\(x_N=0\\), \\(y=B^{-\\top}c_B\\), and reduced costs \\(\\bar c_N=c_N-N^\\top y\\). If \\(x_B\\ge0\\) and \\(\\bar c_N\\ge0\\), then the associated basic feasible solution \\(x\\) is optimal. The basis, primal basic values, and reduced costs constitute a certificate verifiable by solving linear systems and checking componentwise signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis certifies optimality when its basic solution is feasible and every nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative for the minimization convention.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\\in\\mathbb R^{m\\times n}\\) has rank \\(m\\), with \\(b\\in\\mathbb R^m\\) and \\(c\\in\\mathbb R^n\\).
\\(B\\) consists of \\(m\\) linearly independent columns of \\(A\\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basic feasible solution \\(x=(B^{-1}b,0)\\) belongs to \\(\\operatorname*{argmin}\\{c^\\top z:Az=b,\\ z\\ge0\\}\\).

notation.meaning: The basic and nonbasic column matrices.
The dual vector induced by the basis.
